newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: E.EUROPEANS WANT EARLY EU ENTRY BUT ON GOOD TERMS.
newsitem.headline: E.EUROPEANS WANT EARLY EU ENTRY BUT ON GOOD TERMS.

text.p: Eastern European states are sticking to their plans for the earliest possible membership of the European Union, despite mixed signals from Brussels, but say winning the right terms is more important than deadlines.

The European Commission said in a fact sheet on Wednesday, that was later withdrawn and described as "erroneous", that no new members would be admitted before 2002, evoking disappointment in some Eastern European capitals.

"We insist that negotiations can be concluded in 2000 although we realise that full membership could come later, say in 2001," Istvan Szent-Ivanyi, state secretary at Hungary's Foreign Ministry told Reuters on Thursday.
Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland are seen as the leading candidates to be the first new members of the EU, with others, including Slovenia and Slovakia, also eager to join.
The mix-up at the Commission followed a visit to Hungary last week by French President Jacques Chirac, who said there was no reason why Hungary should not be an EU member by 2000.
His Foreign Minister Herve de Charette took a similar message to Prague.
But, despite the symbolism of the new millenium, several states insist that joining on good terms is more important.

"We have a plan, the year 2000. But frankly, if I had to decide whether to enter in 2000 on poorer terms or in 2001 on better terms, I would prefer 2001," Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told a news briefing on Wednesday.

The Czech Foreign Ministry said in a statement after the Commission fact sheet was issued, that any decision on enlargement would be for the council of ministers, but said it had no interest in pushing forward its entry date.
"While the date of entry is being determined, the Czech Foreign Ministry does not want to speed up the timetable, when the negotiation process with the union is just beginning," it said.
"We are in no hurry, we do not want to be the poorest EU member," said parliamentarian Vaclav Najemnik of the Civic Democratic Party, the senior partner in the ruling coalition.
But asked if applicants would be disappointed or confused by the slip at the EU executive, European Commissioner Hans van den Broek said in Prague the situation was clear.
"If they are disappointed, they are certainly not confused because they know exactly what we are talking about," he said.
Van den Broek, the commissioner responsible for relations with Central and Eastern Europe, told a meeting the issue was not if, but when the applicants would become members.
"The when is solely determined by the degree of preparation that the countries will have reached and the time it will need to ratify the results of the negotiations," he said.
Talks on accession are due to begin six months after the EU's inter-governmental conference, which is scheduled to end in June, but this is out of applicant countries' hands.
"We hope to become EU members as soon as possible, but that is not for us to decide," said Ivo Vajgl, a spokesman at Slovenia's foreign ministry.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, speaking in Budapest this week, highlighted the position of East European applicants in discussions on the accession timetable.

"If President Chirac talks before the Polish Parliament about 2000 for Polish membership of the EU, if (German) Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl is speaking about 2000, what can I as the President of Poland say?"
